title.value: Use of Domain Decomposition and Local Grid Refinement in Reservoir Simulation

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: In order to get the desired accuracy in reservoir simulation, it is often necessary to refine the grid in certain regions, for example, the regions around wells. When this is done in conventional simulators, unnecessary refinement occurs in other regions. This problem is avoided by the use of Local Grid Refinement (LGR) techniques, but the resulting matrix is large and of irregular sparsity.In this work, first, several practical aspects of some methods of LGR, including the use of hybrid grid, are addressed and then a new powerful Domain Decomposition (DD) technique is proposed. This proposed method performs domain decomposition at the reservoir level instead of at the matrix level. The proposed method does not exclude the application of the existing methods; it can be considered a new tool, which can be used together with the existing methods for solving reservoir simulation problems. In this proposed method the reservoir it; physically divided into several smaller regions and each one of these regions is solved separately. At the first iteration, when an interface between two subdomains is first encountered, Dirichlet boundary conditions are used. During subsequent iterations and during subsequent encounters of the interface, either Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions can be used. In order to ensure rapid convergence in the outer loop of the algorithm, some acceleration techniques are used.Three highly efficient acceleration methods of solving the resulting problems with DD technique are also proposed. In the first acceleration method, a relaxation in the unknowns is performed. In the second one, overlapping boundaries between the subdomains are used. In the last one, a coarse grid solution is obtained first and it provides the starting boundary conditions for the fine grid solution.The LGR and DD methods developed in this work were implemented and tested in a three-dimensional, three-phase, extended black-oil model. The LGR and DD techniques discussed in this thesis improve the accuracy of reservoir simulation around wells and in other regions of high activity. Using these techniques, one obtains correct well pressure and correct saturation near the well, without the use of well geometric factors or well pseudofunctions. A consequence of this is that water-oil ratio and gas-oil ratio are predicted accurately.Use of LGR with DD has been found to be a powerful technique for reservoir simulation problems. The methods proposed in this work cam easily take advantage of parallel processors.Use of LGR introduces highly irregular grids in certain regions. This thesis also contains an investigation of the accuracy of six different kinds of gridding systems, which are derived from the classical point-distributed and the block-centered methods. The goal is to obtain maximum accuracy for a given number of blocks, and to properly locate grid points with LGR.The point-distributed gridding system is known to minimize the truncation error in the discretization of the pressure derivative (flow terms), whereas the block-centered gridding system is known to minimize the truncation error in the discretization of the volume integral (accumulation terms). When a uniform grid spacing is used both methods minimize the truncation error in the same way, with the truncation error being of second order for midpoint weighted transmissibility and first order for single point upstream weighted transmissibility. However, in many practical problems, it is necessary to refine the grid in certain regions of the reservoir, thus resulting in an irregular grid spacing for the system.Because sometimes the results obtained from an irregularly spaced fine grid are not as accurate as the results obtained from a regularly spaced coarse grid, a truncation error analysis for irregular systems using upstream transmissibility is performed. This analysis shows that both point-distributed and block-centered methods are locally inconsistent; Le., have error of order zero. However, because of the way the block boundaries are selected in the point-distributed and related techniques, these methods give more accurate results when compared with block-centered and related methods.
Nacul, Evandro Correa. (1991). Use of Domain Decomposition and Local Grid Refinement in Reservoir Simulation. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/mw414ng0531
